identification.summary: Hazel Sandstorm (formerly EUROPIUM) is an Iranian actor that Microsoft says has been publicly linked to Iran's Ministry of Intelligence and Security (MOIS) [S1][S2]. Microsoft assessed with moderate confidence that actors linked to it gained initial access to the Albanian government and exfiltrated data before Iran's destructive attack there in July 2022 [S1][S2]. Other vendors track overlapping activity as APT34/OilRig, Crambus or Earth Simnavaz. That reporting describes long-running espionage against Middle East governments using PowerShell and .NET backdoors, Exchange-based C2, DNS tunneling, web shells and credential theft [S3][S4][S5][S6][S7].
identification.firstObserved: Microsoft: DEV-0861, which it links to EUROPIUM, has been exfiltrating mail from several countries since April 2020 [S2]. FireEye reported APT34 use of CVE-2017-0199 by July 2017 [S3].
identification.notes: Microsoft name: Hazel Sandstorm (formerly EUROPIUM). Microsoft tracks EUROPIUM through three activity clusters with distinct tools or TTPs, some of which may work for the same unit [S2]. FireEye said APT34 'loosely aligns' with public OilRig reporting [S3]. Trend Micro equates Earth Simnavaz with APT34/OilRig [S6]. Symantec tracks the group as Crambus [S5]. These vendor clusters overlap but are not proven identical. Microsoft's link to Storm-0861 (DEV-0861) carries only moderate confidence [S2].

attribution.sponsor: Iran. Microsoft says EUROPIUM/Hazel Sandstorm has been publicly linked to the Ministry of Intelligence and Security (MOIS) [S1][S2]. Check Point also associates APT34 with MOIS [S7].
attribution.confidence: Microsoft judged with high confidence that the 15 July 2022 destructive attack on Albania was carried out by Iranian state-sponsored actors. Its link from the initial-access and exfiltration actors to EUROPIUM is moderate confidence [S2]. FireEye assessed APT34 as a suspected Iranian cyber-espionage group [S3]. No government attribution document was reviewed for this record.
attribution.basis: Microsoft incident response and telemetry, including shared RawDisk license keys and code-signing certificates across Albanian and Middle East intrusions [S2]. Vendor malware and infrastructure analysis (FireEye, ESET, Symantec, Check Point, Trend Micro), including code overlaps with earlier Karkoff and Saitama tools [S3][S4][S5][S6][S7].

objectives: Strategic espionage against regional governments and critical sectors in support of Iranian state interests [S2][S5][S6][S7]. This includes long-dwell collection of email, files and credentials [S2][S5]. Microsoft also places it in enabling roles for destructive and retaliatory operations, as in Albania in 2022 [S2].

regions: Israel, Jordan, Kuwait, Saudi Arabia, Turkey, UAE [S2]
targeting.notes: Microsoft lists the EUROPIUM target countries as consistent with Iranian interests [S2]. Microsoft's Hazel Sandstorm profile lists only Albania and government [S1]. The broader regional picture comes from vendor clusters that overlap with it [S4][S5][S6][S7].

capabilities.summary: Initial access: unpatched internet-facing servers, including SharePoint CVE-2019-0604 (Albania), plus ProxyLogon CVE-2021-26855 cited in the same intrusion [S2]. Also rapidly weaponized Office exploits CVE-2017-0199 and CVE-2017-11882, the latter used within a week of its patch [S3]. Spearphishing with VBS droppers and double-extension lures [S4][S7]. Post-exploitation: web shells, Mimikatz, Impacket and RDP [S2]. Malicious password-filter DLLs and the StealHook backdoor for credential theft, and CVE-2024-30088 for privilege escalation [S6]. Backdoors include POWRUNER and BONDUPDATER [S3], Solar and Mango [S4], PowerExchange [S5], and Veaty and Spearal [S7]. C2 options: email or Exchange-based channels (EWS, compromised internal mailboxes) [S4][S5][S7], custom DNS tunneling [S7], compromised legitimate websites [S4] and ngrok tunneling [S6]. Collection: Exchange mailbox exfiltration [S2][S5][S6], browser and Windows Credential Manager theft [S4]. The 2019 Lab Dookhtegan leak exposed APT34 tools (Glimpse, PoisonFrog, HyperShell, HighShell, Fox Panel, Webmask), plus later the Jason brute-force tool [S8]. Microsoft notes Jason.exe was used by MOIS-affiliated actors in Albania (DEV-0166) [S2][S8].

campaigns.name: APT34 CVE-2017-0199 campaign
campaigns.summary: FireEye reported that APT34 used malicious RTF files exploiting CVE-2017-0199 to deliver the POWRUNER backdoor and a DGA-capable downloader.

campaigns.name: APT34 CVE-2017-11882 exploitation
campaigns.summary: Less than a week after the patch, FireEye saw APT34 exploit the Office Equation Editor flaw against a Middle East government organization, deploying POWRUNER and BONDUPDATER.

campaigns.name: Lab Dookhtegan leaks
campaigns.summary: A Telegram persona leaked APT34 tool source code, infrastructure details and data on 66 victims. Chronicle confirmed the tools were authentic, and the Jason tool followed in June 2019.

campaigns.name: ZeroCleare-related access (Middle East energy)
campaigns.summary: Microsoft cites IBM X-Force's assessment that EUROPIUM-affiliated actors gained access to a Middle East energy company nearly a year before a ZeroCleare wiper attack.

campaigns.name: Outer Space (Israel)
campaigns.summary: ESET reports that OilRig used the Solar backdoor and the EWS-based SC5k downloader, with compromised Israeli websites as C2.

campaigns.name: Albania government intrusion (Storm-0861 / DEV-0861)
campaigns.summary: Access came through SharePoint CVE-2019-0604 in May 2021 and was consolidated in July 2021. Mail was exfiltrated from October 2021 to January 2022, and a separate Iranian actor conducted the destructive attack on 15 July 2022. Microsoft links the access and exfiltration actors to EUROPIUM with moderate confidence.

campaigns.name: Juicy Mix (Israel)
campaigns.summary: ESET reports that OilRig deployed the Mango backdoor, a successor to Solar, along with browser and credential stealers.

campaigns.name: Crambus eight-month government intrusion
campaigns.summary: Symantec reports intrusion into an unnamed Middle East government from February to September 2023 using the PowerExchange email-based backdoor.

campaigns.name: Iraq government campaign (Veaty/Spearal)
campaigns.summary: Check Point reports attacks on Iraqi government networks using email-C2 Veaty and DNS-tunneling Spearal malware, with lures branded as the Iraqi General Secretariat of the Council of Ministers.

campaigns.name: Earth Simnavaz Gulf campaign
campaigns.summary: Trend Micro reports web-shell access to UAE and Gulf government targets, followed by CVE-2024-30088 privilege escalation, a password-filter DLL, the StealHook backdoor and Exchange credential abuse.

diamond.adversary: An Iranian actor that Microsoft says has been publicly linked to MOIS, tracked as Hazel Sandstorm/EUROPIUM [S1][S2], with overlapping vendor clusters APT34/OilRig, Crambus and Earth Simnavaz [S3][S5][S6]. Personnel and tools were exposed by the 2019 Lab Dookhtegan leaks [S8].
diamond.capability: Server and Office exploits (CVE-2019-0604, CVE-2017-0199, CVE-2017-11882), web shells, credential theft (Mimikatz, password-filter DLLs, StealHook), privilege escalation via CVE-2024-30088, and custom .NET/PowerShell backdoors with email and DNS C2 [S2][S3][S4][S5][S6][S7].
diamond.infrastructure: Exfiltration IPs on hosting providers listed by Microsoft [S2]. Compromised legitimate websites used as C2 [S4], compromised internal Exchange mailboxes used for C2 [S5][S7], DNS tunneling [S7] and ngrok tunnels [S6].
diamond.victim: Governments in Albania, Iraq, the UAE and Gulf, and an unnamed Middle East state [S2][S5][S6][S7]. Israeli organizations [S4]. A Middle East energy company [S2].
diamond.socioPolitical: Iranian regional intelligence priorities and retaliation. Microsoft assessed that Tehran likely used the Albania attacks as retaliation [S2].
diamond.technology: Microsoft Exchange and EWS, on-premises SharePoint, Windows domain controllers and password filters, and Windows privilege-escalation flaws [S2][S4][S5][S6].

gaps: MITRE mapping conflict: this actor record carries G0003 (Cleaver), but OilRig is MITRE G0049. The imported Cleaver/Operation Cleaver aliases and software (TinyZBot, Net Crawler) were not verified against Microsoft's Hazel Sandstorm mapping in this research.
Microsoft's link from Storm-0861/DEV-0861 to EUROPIUM is moderate confidence, and how Microsoft's three EUROPIUM clusters map onto APT34/OilRig, Crambus and Earth Simnavaz is not public [S2].
No US or allied government attribution document naming Hazel Sandstorm/APT34 was opened. The FBI/CISA Albania advisory was not reviewed (government sites are blocked).
Symantec's primary Crambus report was not opened directly; the details come from search-result coverage [S5].
The initial access vector is unknown for the Crambus (2023) and Iraq (2024) campaigns [S5][S7].
Reports of 2025 activity and of AI-tool use (aggregator sources) were not verified against primary vendor reporting.
Unit 42's original OilRig reporting (2016 onward) and Mandiant's 2019 LinkedIn phishing reporting were not reviewed for dates.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1: Key terrain is internet-facing Exchange and SharePoint servers, domain controllers (where password filters can be installed), and mail flows of partner-nation governments in the Gulf, Iraq, Israel and Albania [S2][S5][S6][S7]. STEP 2: Fast weaponization of Office and server CVEs and long dwell times (8 months in the Crambus case; 8+ months from access to the destructive phase in Albania) favor the adversary where patching is slow [S2][S3][S5]. STEP 3: The doctrinal template runs from server exploit or spearphish to web shell or backdoor, then credential theft (Mimikatz, password-filter DLL), then Exchange mailbox collection over email or DNS C2 [S2][S4][S5][S6][S7]. STEP 4: MLCOA is persistent email and credential espionage against host-nation and coalition partner ministries. MDCOA is Hazel Sandstorm-enabled access handed to a separate Iranian destructive actor for wiper or ransomware effects during a crisis, as in Albania 2022 [S2]. Candidate indicators: new ASPX web shells on SharePoint or Exchange, unexpected LSA notification-package or password-filter DLL registrations, EWS impersonation-role grants or service accounts, anomalous DNS TXT/subdomain volume, ngrok binaries or traffic, and double-extension document attachments [S2][S6][S7].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Situational awareness: partner-nation government mail systems in the CENTCOM AOR are a recurring target. JCC2 should fuse partner CERT reporting and coalition mail-gateway telemetry, since the actor uses victims' own Exchange mailboxes for C2 [S5][S7]. (2) Authorities: activity often sits on partner, not DoD, networks, so response depends on partner-nation consent and established information-sharing agreements. (3) Mission assurance: an espionage foothold can enable a destructive handoff to another actor [S2]. Treat detected Hazel Sandstorm access in mission-relevant networks as a potential precursor to disruptive effects, not espionage only. (4) Coordination: attribution across overlapping vendor names is inconsistent, so coordinate with the intelligence community and partners on indicators rather than labels, and prioritize Exchange/SharePoint patching and credential resets.
